reason: While the text does demonstrate Jacob's concern for the welfare of those under his care—particularly evident in Genesis 33:13-14, where he declines Esau's offer to travel together, citing the tender condition of the children and nursing livestock and explaining he must travel slowly 'at the pace of the droves before me and at the pace of the children'—the passage does not present this as a prescriptive 'model for good leadership.' The text is primarily narrative in character, focusing on Jacob's reconciliation with Esau following his encounter with the divine at Penuel. Jacob's care for his dependents is shown as a practical necessity and personal concern rather than as an exemplary leadership principle that is explicitly taught or held up as a model to follow.
